WASHINGTON (CNN) -- U.S., Turkish and Iraqi leaders all held talks Monday about Kurdish rebels using northern Iraq as a launchpad for cross-border attacks into Turkey. Turkish troops patrol near the border with Iraq on Monday. President Bush chatted by phone with Turkish Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan, while separately two senior Iraq national government figures met with the head of the country's Kurdish region. The diplomatic moves came after Turkish warplanes pounded Kurdish separatist targets in northern Iraq on Saturday and Sunday as well as last week. Bush and Erdogan talked about the dangers of the Kurdish separatist rebels along the Turkish-Iraqi border, the White House confirmed. National Security Council spokesman Gordon Johndroe said they discussed their common efforts to fight terrorism, and the importance of the United States, Turkey and Iraq working together to confront the Kurdistan Workers' Party, or PKK. Bush has vowed to help Turkey fight PKK rebels. The PKK has spent two decades fighting for autonomy for Kurds in southeastern Turkey, with some of its attacks launched from inside northern Iraq. The United States and European Union consider the group a terrorist organization. Last week, Turkey's ambassador to the United States, Nabi Sensoy, said his country's maneuvers against Kurdish militant targets in northern Iraq were based on intelligence provided by the United States. In the Kurdish Iraq city of Sulaimaniya, Iraqi President Jalal Talabani, who is Kurdish, and Vice President Tariq al-Hashimi, who is Sunni Arab, met with Kurdish Regional Government President Massoud Barzani. Iraqi Kurdish officials, while critical of the PKK, have denounced the Turkish bombing campaign. Last week, Barzani snubbed visiting U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice in protest of the attacks. "We have vehemently condemned the bombardment. The bombing targeted safe and secure areas and innocent people. Several people were either killed or wounded," Barzani said on Monday at a press conference with the others. "We held consultations with President Jalal Talabani and we will continue our consultations with other concerned parties to put an end to these aggressions and put to an end the shelling of villages." The three Iraqi officials also dealt with national unity. They signed a "memorandum of understanding" to deepen relations further with their three parties: Talabani's Patriotic Union of Kurdistan, Barzani's Kurdistan Democratic Party and al-Hashimi's Iraqi Islamic Party, a Sunni Arab entity. E-mail to a friend . CNN's Kathleen Koch, Talia Kayali and Mohammed Tawfeeq contributed to this report .

President Bush spoke by telephone with Turkish Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan, while, in a separate development, two senior figures from Iraq's national government met with the head of the country's Kurdish region. These diplomatic efforts followed a series of Turkish airstrikes against Kurdish separatist targets in northern Iraq, which were carried out on Saturday and Sunday, as well as earlier in the week.

According to the White House, Bush and Erdogan discussed the threat posed by Kurdish separatist rebels operating along the Turkish-Iraqi border. National Security Council spokesman Gordon Johndroe stated that the two leaders addressed their joint efforts to combat terrorism and emphasized the importance of cooperation among the United States, Turkey, and Iraq in confronting the Kurdistan Workers' Party, or PKK. Bush has pledged to assist Turkey in its fight against PKK rebels.

For two decades, the PKK has waged a campaign for Kurdish autonomy in southeastern Turkey, launching some of its attacks from within northern Iraq. Both the United States and the European Union classify the group as a terrorist organization. Last week, Turkey's ambassador to the United States, Nabi Sensoy, revealed that his country's operations against Kurdish militant targets in northern Iraq were based on intelligence supplied by the United States.

In the Iraqi Kurdish city of Sulaimaniya, Iraqi President Jalal Talabani, a Kurd, and Vice President Tariq al-Hashimi, a Sunni Arab, met with Kurdish Regional Government President Massoud Barzani. While critical of the PKK, Iraqi Kurdish officials have condemned the Turkish bombing campaign. Last week, Barzani declined to meet with visiting U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice in protest of the attacks.

"We have vehemently condemned the bombardment. The bombing targeted safe and secure areas and innocent people. Several people were either killed or wounded," Barzani said Monday at a press conference held alongside the other officials. "We held consultations with President Jalal Talabani, and we will continue our consultations with other concerned parties to put an end to these aggressions and to the shelling of villages."

The three Iraqi officials also addressed the matter of national unity. Both leaders emphasized the importance of cooperation among the United States, Turkey, and Iraq in confronting the group, signaling a coordinated approach to the security threat.

These diplomatic efforts came in the wake of Turkish military action against Kurdish separatist targets in northern Iraq. Over the weekend, as well as during the preceding week, Turkey had conducted airstrikes on positions believed to be associated with the rebels, intensifying the urgency of the diplomatic engagement.

# US, Turkey, Iraq Hold Talks Amid Rising Tensions Over Kurdish PKK Rebels

**Diplomatic efforts intensify as Turkish airstrikes in northern Iraq strain regional relations**

Senior officials from the United States, Turkey, and Iraq convened this week for high-level diplomatic talks aimed at addressing the ongoing conflict surrounding Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) militants operating in northern Iraq, a situation that has increasingly complicated relations among the three governments.

The meetings come after a series of Turkish military operations targeting PKK positions in the mountainous border regions of northern Iraq, strikes that Ankara says are necessary for its national security but which Baghdad has criticized as violations of Iraqi sovereignty.

## Competing Security Interests

Turkey has long considered the PKK a terrorist organization, a designation shared by the United States and European Union. The group has waged an insurgency against the Turkish state for decades, with the conflict claiming tens of thousands of lives since the 1980s.

"Turkey has legitimate security concerns that must be addressed," a State Department official said, speaking on condition of anonymity. "At the same time, we recognize the importance of respecting Iraqi territorial integrity and working through coordinated channels."

Iraqi officials have expressed frustration over the cross-border operations, arguing that unilateral military action undermines their authority and endangers civilians in the Kurdistan Region.

## The U.S. Balancing Act

Washington finds itself in a delicate position, balancing its alliance with Turkey—a fellow NATO member—against its partnership with Iraq and Kurdish forces who have been key allies in operations against ISIS.

Analysts note that the United States has sought to encourage cooperation rather than confrontation. "The U.S. wants to prevent this from escalating into a broader crisis that could destabilize the region," said one regional security expert. "There's a real interest in finding mechanisms that address Turkey's concerns while maintaining Iraq's cooperation."

## Path Forward Uncertain

While the talks reportedly produced commitments to enhance intelligence sharing and border security coordination, significant differences remain. Turkish officials have signaled they will continue operations against PKK targets, while Iraqi representatives pressed for greater consultation and respect for their sovereignty.

The Kurdistan Regional Government, which governs the semi-autonomous northern region where much of the fighting occurs, has walked a careful line, condemning PKK activities that draw Turkish military responses while also objecting to strikes that affect its territory.

Whether the diplomatic engagement will yield lasting results remains to be seen, as the underlying tensions surrounding the PKK's presence and Turkey's response continue to test relationships in one of the world's most volatile regions.

# Turkey Steps Up Pressure on PKK as U.S. Offers Intelligence Support

**ANKARA, Turkey (CNN)** — Tensions along Turkey's mountainous border with northern Iraq intensified this week as Turkish forces conducted cross-border strikes against Kurdish rebel positions, while Washington moved to expand intelligence-sharing with its NATO ally in an effort to head off a broader military incursion.

The escalation follows a series of deadly attacks by the Kurdistan Workers' Party, or PKK, which has killed dozens of Turkish soldiers in recent weeks. The group, designated a terrorist organization by Turkey, the United States and the European Union, has waged a decades-long insurgency that has claimed an estimated 30,000 lives since 1984.

## Washington Walks a Diplomatic Tightrope

The Bush administration has found itself caught between two allies, seeking to reassure Turkey of its commitment while protecting the relative stability of Iraqi Kurdistan — one of the few calmer regions in an otherwise turbulent Iraq.

Following talks in Washington, U.S. officials confirmed that intelligence cooperation with Turkey would be enhanced, including the sharing of real-time information on PKK movements gathered through surveillance and reconnaissance assets.

"We consider the PKK a common enemy," a senior administration official told reporters, speaking on condition of anonymity. "We are committed to working with our Turkish partners, but we also urge restraint to avoid destabilizing the region."

Turkish officials, however, have expressed frustration with what they describe as insufficient action by both Washington and Baghdad against rebel camps operating in the Qandil Mountains.

## Turkish Military Presses Operations

Turkey's parliament earlier authorized the government to launch cross-border operations into northern Iraq, giving Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan's government a one-year mandate for military action.

Turkish artillery has shelled suspected rebel positions, and warplanes have targeted PKK hideouts near the border. The military reported killing a number of militants in the operations, though independent verification remained difficult in the remote terrain.

Erdogan has faced mounting domestic pressure to respond forcefully to the attacks, with public anger swelling after the deaths of Turkish troops.

"Turkey has the right to defend itself," Erdogan said, while adding that his government preferred a coordinated approach with the United States and Iraq.

## Iraqi Kurds Caught in the Middle

The crisis has placed Iraq's Kurdish leadership in a difficult position. Massoud Barzani, president of the Kurdistan Regional Government, condemned PKK attacks but resisted Turkish demands for a crackdown, warning against any incursion into Iraqi territory.

"We will not hand over anyone," Barzani said, while urging both sides to pursue dialogue. "But we are also opposed to violence and terrorism from any party."

Iraqi Kurdish officials have called for a political solution, arguing that a large-scale Turkish military operation would harm civilians and threaten the region's fragile stability.

Baghdad's central government, meanwhile, has pledged to close PKK offices and restrict the group's activities, though critics question whether it has the capacity to enforce such measures in the semi-autonomous north.

## What Lies Ahead

Analysts warn that a major Turkish incursion could complicate U.S. operations in Iraq and strain relations between Washington and Ankara at a sensitive time.

For now, diplomatic efforts continue, with U.S. officials shuttling between the capitals in hopes of preventing a wider conflict. But with public pressure high in Turkey and rebel attacks persisting, the coming weeks may prove decisive.

*CNN's correspondents in Ankara, Baghdad and Washington contributed to this report.*

# International Coalition Weighs New Steps to Confront Kurdistan Workers' Party

*By Sarah Whitman and Daniel Rourke, with additional reporting by Leyla Demir in Istanbul and Michael Foss in Brussels*

**WASHINGTON** — Senior diplomats from the United States, Turkey and several European governments gathered here this week to coordinate a renewed strategy toward the Kurdistan Workers' Party, or PKK, as officials assess how to respond to shifting conditions on the ground in the group's longtime strongholds across the Turkey-Iraq border.

The talks, held over two days at the State Department, brought together counterterrorism officials and regional envoys seeking to align their approaches to an organization that Washington, Ankara and the European Union have long designated a terrorist group. The PKK has waged an armed insurgency against the Turkish state since 1984, a conflict that has killed tens of thousands of people.

"There is broad agreement that the moment calls for a coordinated posture," a senior U.S. official told reporters on condition of anonymity because the discussions were private. "That includes financial pressure, close intelligence cooperation and support for a durable political resolution."

## A Shifting Landscape

The consultations come amid renewed attention to the decades-old conflict, following a series of statements from PKK-affiliated figures signaling a potential willingness to move away from armed struggle. Analysts caution that previous cease-fires and peace initiatives have collapsed, and that skepticism remains high on all sides.

Turkish officials have pressed their international partners to maintain sustained pressure on the group's financing networks and its logistical presence in northern Iraq, where the PKK maintains bases in mountainous terrain. Ankara has conducted repeated cross-border military operations in the region, drawing both support and concern from neighboring governments.

"Turkey expects its allies to treat this threat with the seriousness it deserves," a Turkish foreign ministry spokesperson said in a statement. "Coordination on terrorism financing and the movement of fighters is essential."

## European Caution

European participants struck a more measured tone, emphasizing the need to distinguish between the PKK as a designated organization and broader Kurdish political and civil movements, which are legal and represented in parliaments across the region.

"Our commitment to the terrorist designation is firm, but so is our commitment to human rights and to a political process," said a European Commission official involved in the Brussels-Washington coordination. Rights organizations have urged governments to ensure that counterterrorism measures do not translate into broader restrictions on Kurdish civil society, journalists or elected officials.

Humanitarian groups have separately warned that continued instability in the border regions threatens displaced populations and complicates reconstruction efforts in areas affected by years of fighting.

## Questions Over Iraq and Syria

Much of the discussion, participants said, centered on the complex geography of the conflict, which spans Turkey, Iraq and Syria. U.S. officials face the delicate task of maintaining ties with Kurdish-led forces in northeastern Syria — key partners in operations against the Islamic State — while addressing Turkish concerns about links between those forces and the PKK. Ankara regards several of those groups as extensions of the PKK, a characterization the groups themselves reject.

Baghdad, meanwhile, has sought to reassert authority over its northern territory and has publicly restricted PKK activity, though the group's presence in the semi-autonomous Kurdistan Region of Iraq remains a persistent source of friction.

"The regional picture is deeply interconnected," said Elif Karadag, a fellow at a Washington-based policy institute who studies the conflict. "Any strategy that treats these theaters in isolation is likely to run into trouble."

## Next Steps

Officials said the participating governments agreed to convene a follow-up working group in the coming months and to expand information-sharing on financial networks. No formal agreement was announced, and several delegates cautioned that meaningful progress would depend on developments beyond the negotiating table.

For now, participants described the meetings as an effort to keep partners aligned during an uncertain period.

"The goal," the senior U.S. official said, "is to be prepared for multiple scenarios — including the possibility of a genuine turn away from violence, and the possibility that it does not materialize."

---
